buttonLabel: "Explore the culture of Brazil, Peru and Uruguay"
lead: >-
  Rio de Janeiro's historic center, a one-day excursion in Montevideo and Inca monuments from Cusco to Machu Picchu offer three different perspectives on South American culture. Our current selection includes journeys through six and eight countries: Brazil, Peru and Uruguay are principal destinations, but other countries are obligatory stages between them.
---

## What the cultural and historical itineraries include

Our catalog features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}: a [20-day journey through six countries](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) and a [32-day route through eight countries](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/). Both visit [Brazil](/brazil/), [Uruguay](/uruguay/) and [Peru](/peru/), but **neither is a standalone three-country tour**. Between Uruguay and Peru, travelers cross Chile and Bolivia; after Lima, the longer itinerary continues to Ecuador and Colombia.

For a culturally curious traveler, the main difference between the three selected countries is the depth of the experience. Rio features city sightseeing, Montevideo is allocated one day, and Peru includes several consecutive historical stops: Titicaca, Cusco, Machu Picchu and Lima.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_latin_america_six_countries_20_days_2026,tour_south_america_eight_countries_32_days_2026}}

The [general Brazil, Peru and Uruguay selection](/multi-country/brazil_peru_uruguay/) explains the full logistics. Here we focus on historical landmarks and cultural experiences. Other routes are available in the [multi-country culture and history catalog](/multi-country/interests/culture-and-history/).

## Brazil: the history and architecture of Rio de Janeiro

In [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/), travelers visit Corcovado and Christ the Redeemer, Sugarloaf Mountain and the central districts. A sightseeing tour includes the cathedral and buildings associated with the city's colonial history. The urban landscape constantly meets the bay and steep green slopes, a relationship especially visible from the viewpoints.

The itinerary offers a substantial first introduction but **is not a separate multi-day museum tour**. After Rio, travelers continue to [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/), where waterfalls and tropical forest become the focus. Anyone primarily interested in Brazilian art, music and museums should compare [Brazil tours](/brazil/tour/) and discuss extra days in Rio.

## Uruguay: one day in Montevideo

Travelers arrive in [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) by ferry from [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/). A vehicle-based tour of the capital takes in the port, Independence Square, central neighborhoods, the Old Town and cathedral. The group then returns by ferry.

This format lets visitors compare two cities on opposite shores of the Río de la Plata and gain a first impression of Uruguay. But **these itineraries do not include an overnight stay in Montevideo** or extra days for the country's museums and historical towns. If Uruguay is your main cultural objective, extending your stay is more sensible than fitting everything around a one-day ferry excursion.

This is an international crossing, so the ferry schedule, documents, entry rules for each nationality and border-processing time all need checking. They determine how much time is actually available to see the sights.

## Peru: from Titicaca to Machu Picchu and Lima

Peru's stage is considerably richer. The journey passes through [Puno and Lake Titicaca](/peru/place/puno-and-lake-titicaca/), with a visit to the [Uros Islands](/peru/place/uros-islands/), towards [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/). Here travelers discover Inca heritage and monuments of later eras.

The key historical stop is [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/). Stone buildings and terraces, set among the mountains, reveal Inca engineering traditions. UNESCO recognizes the site's historical and natural significance. A visit requires a ticket for a particular route and time, so it needs to be coordinated with the train journey in advance.

In [Lima](/peru/place/lima/), the itinerary turns to the capital's historic neighborhoods. Along with Cusco and Titicaca, this produces a sequence of historical experiences rather than a single short visit to a famous archaeological site.

## Tiwanaku: why the history extends beyond the three selected countries

Before reaching Peru, both tours pass through Bolivia. After high-altitude travel, visitors explore [La Paz](/bolivia/place/la-paz/) and [Tiwanaku](/bolivia/place/tiwanaku/). Tiwanaku belongs to a distinct pre-Columbian Andean civilization that existed before the Inca period; its ceremonial architecture is included on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

This makes the cultural journey richer by offering an opportunity to compare different ancient Altiplano societies with the later monuments of Cusco. Removing Bolivia would mean losing not just a geographical stage but also this significant historical stop.

## Choosing between the two durations

The principal cultural experiences in Rio, Montevideo and Peru are similar in both programs. The 32-day option has broader geography: after Peru, travelers visit Ecuador, where [Quito](/ecuador/place/quito-and-cotopaxi-volcano/) has a historic-center tour and a visit to the equator line, followed by Colombia. These extra days do not increase the time spent in Uruguay.

The 20-day tour ends in Lima and takes fewer calendar days. When choosing, compare not only duration but also guide languages, early departures, mountain transfers and actual sightseeing hours. More options on this theme appear in the [“Culture and History” section](/interests/culture-and-history/).

## Frequently asked questions about cultural tours

### Is there an overnight stay in Montevideo?

No. Both existing itineraries include a one-day ferry excursion from Buenos Aires with a return the same day.

### Are Cusco and Machu Picchu included in both tours?

Yes. [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/) and [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/) are included in both routes. The timing of the archaeological visit and transport arrangements are agreed in advance.

### Why is Bolivia part of a cultural journey through these countries?

Because the route includes [Tiwanaku](/bolivia/place/tiwanaku/), with monuments belonging to an ancient civilization distinct from that of the Incas.

### Can the trip cover only three countries?

A tailor-made journey can be discussed, but it would be a different program. The existing tours also cross Argentina, Chile and Bolivia, and their transport arrangements cannot be shortened without recalculating the journey.

targetPath: /multi-country/brazil_peru_uruguay/interests/food-and-wine/
kind: multi_country_interest
status: approved
locale: en
buttonLabel: "Explore food and wine in Brazil, Peru and Uruguay"
lead: >-
  Brazil, Peru and Uruguay offer three distinct culinary traditions: everyday food in Rio, vibrant flavors in Lima, and grilled meats with Tannat wine in Montevideo. On Ada Tours' current 20-day itinerary, these countries belong to a six-nation journey. The program includes a tango-show dinner in Argentina and the option of visiting Maipo Valley wineries in Chile. Separate tastings in Brazil, Peru and Uruguay, however, are not included in the standard itinerary. Here we explain where to try local cuisine independently and how to arrange a genuine culinary journey.
---

## Three countries' cuisine: what the existing tour includes

Our food-and-wine selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. One itinerary is the [20-day tour through six Latin American countries](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/): [Brazil](/brazil/), Argentina, [Uruguay](/uruguay/), Chile, Bolivia and [Peru](/peru/). It links Rio de Janeiro, Iguazú, Buenos Aires, Montevideo, Santiago, Atacama, Uyuni, Titicaca, Cusco, Machu Picchu and Lima.

**The “Food and Wine” label applies to the entire six-country program.** It does not mean that each of the three selected countries is visited on a tasting or wine tour. The confirmed gastronomic experiences are distributed as follows:

- In Buenos Aires, **Argentina**, a tango show with dinner is planned, serving traditional dishes and Argentine wine.
- In Santiago, **Chile**, travelers can optionally visit wineries in the Maipo Valley for a tasting; the stated price is **$230 per person, minimum 2 participants**.
- In Rio, Montevideo and Lima, travelers can explore local food during free time, but dedicated culinary excursions in those cities are not included in the standard tour.

This distinction is important when choosing the right format. The existing itinerary is well suited to discovering the geography and culture of six countries. A journey centered on restaurants, cooking classes and wineries requires different priorities and perhaps extra days.

The [Brazil + Peru + Uruguay selection](/multi-country/brazil_peru_uruguay/) shows the complete geographical context. This page focuses specifically on food, wine and free time in the three named countries.

## Brazil: what to taste in Rio de Janeiro

In [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/), travelers visit Corcovado and Christ the Redeemer, Sugarloaf Mountain and the city's neighborhoods. Between sightseeing excursions, they can try Brazilian cuisine, known for combinations of beans, rice, meat, fish, tropical fruit and local snacks.

A classic example is **feijoada**, a hearty dish made with black beans and meat. Small fried snacks are common in city cafés, while cold mate tea and crunchy cassava-starch *biscoito de polvilho* are popular on beaches and promenades. For a more substantial dinner, choose a restaurant serving Brazilian meat or fish dishes.

Rio offers a culinary experience without traveling to another province: choose a suitable dinner venue after a daytime excursion. But **no particular restaurant, food-market visit or cooking lesson is confirmed in this itinerary**. The venue and timing have to be arranged separately around that day's schedule.

After Rio, the group heads to [Iguazú Falls](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/), where nature excursions take priority. A busy sightseeing schedule and the onward crossing to the Argentine side leave less time for separate culinary outings. Any tasting in this region would need specific arrangements rather than simply replacing the lunch already planned.

If your goal is an in-depth exploration of Brazilian cuisine, discuss adding time in Rio. This creates room for a proper food-focused part of the journey without having to choose between the included excursions and a leisurely dinner.

## Uruguay: Montevideo, grilled meat and Tannat wine

[Uruguay](/uruguay/) is known for its meat cuisine, the *asado* tradition and winemaking. The **Tannat** grape in particular plays an important role in local wine culture. Several wine-growing areas, including those around the capital and in southern Uruguay, have wineries offering visits and tastings.

On this tour, however, [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) is visited **on a one-day trip from Buenos Aires**: a morning ferry across the Río de la Plata, a sightseeing tour of the port, Independence Square, Old Town and cathedral, free time and an evening ferry back. This is an introduction to the capital, not an overnight wine tour.

During the short stay, you might choose a local restaurant if the excursion and ferry timetable allow. Traditional grilled meat, beef dishes and a glass of Uruguayan wine offer a first taste of the country. But **a winery tasting is not included in the current excursion**.

A proper wine day needs different arrangements. You have to select a particular winery, confirm visit and tasting availability, allow for travel from Montevideo and avoid an overly tight schedule around the return ferry. A separate day and possibly an overnight stay in Uruguay are more practical. That would be a tailor-made program, not part of the published standard itinerary.

If Tannat is of particular interest, tell Ada Tours in advance. We can then discuss a winery stage as a distinct travel objective, with agreed guidance and sufficient time for tastings.

## Peru: Lima as the main culinary opportunity

In [Peru](/peru/), the existing itinerary begins around [Puno and Titicaca](/peru/place/puno-and-lake-titicaca/), continues to [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/) and [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/), and ends in [Lima](/peru/place/lima/). The main excursions focus on culture, architecture and archaeology.

Peruvian cuisine deserves special attention for the way it combines Andean traditions with European, African and Asian influences. In Lima, try **ceviche**, fish or seafood in citrus dressing, and **tiradito**, made with thinly sliced fish. Popular hot dishes include **lomo saltado**, combining beef, vegetables and potatoes, while **causa limeña**, made with potatoes, is a characteristic appetizer.

Lima offers Peruvian restaurants, *cevicherías*, small family establishments and restaurants blending Peruvian and Asian culinary traditions. But the existing 20-day tour ends with city sightseeing and a transfer to the airport. **No dedicated ceviche tasting, food-market visit or dinner with a particular chef is listed as included**.

The key question when choosing a culinary experience is whether there is enough free time after seeing Miraflores and the historic center. For an extended tasting menu, especially in a restaurant requiring advance reservations, an additional night in Lima would be more convenient. It would also keep the food experience separate from travel and preparations for an international flight.

Cusco also offers opportunities to discover Andean ingredients and traditional dishes, but several days of this itinerary are devoted to Machu Picchu and visits to historic monuments. A packed sightseeing schedule should not be described as a prearranged culinary tour.

## Where wine and dinner are actually included on the full route

The “Food and Wine” interest on the current [six-country journey](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) has two particularly concrete foundations **outside the selected trio**.

In [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/), an evening tango performance with dinner is included. This is a cultural experience with a culinary component: visitors watch the show and enjoy Argentine dishes with wine. The evening is genuinely part of the itinerary, but it belongs geographically to **Argentina**, not Uruguay.

In Chile, after sightseeing in Santiago, there is an optional excursion to Maipo Valley wineries with a tasting. The published additional charge is **$230 per person for at least two participants**. Do not confuse this option with Uruguayan wineries or count it as an automatically included service.

If you would like to compare the wine traditions of Chile and Uruguay, that could make an interesting custom journey. The current itinerary, however, contains only an optional wine day in Chile. A tasting in Uruguay would need to be added separately; comparing several wineries requires a more relaxed schedule.

## Which culinary format suits you best?

| Goal | Most convenient location | Status on the existing tour |
|---|---|---|
| Local dishes after sightseeing | Rio de Janeiro | Choose a restaurant independently |
| Uruguayan asado and Tannat | Montevideo | No included tasting |
| Ceviche and modern Peruvian cuisine | Lima | No dedicated food tour |
| Dinner and a show | Buenos Aires | Tango show and dinner included |
| Winery and tasting | Maipo Valley, Chile | Optional, $230 per person |

The table distinguishes the opportunity to taste local food from a confirmed tour-operator service. A culinary holiday benefits from preselected venues, defined visiting times and the freedom to enjoy a meal over several hours. On a six-country journey, an occasional free evening does not always provide that opportunity.

If Peruvian food is your main interest, extra days in Lima make sense. For wine travel across several countries, extend the time in Chile or Uruguay. One evening in Rio may be enough to sample Brazilian dishes, but a cooking class requires advance arrangements.

## Practical details: reservations and restrictions

The full tour involves many flights and early departures. When planning restaurants, consider the time you reach the hotel, the length of excursions, the journey to the restaurant and an early start the next day. Lunches and dinners explicitly specified in the itinerary are included as confirmed; additional dishes, drinks and restaurants are paid for separately.

For winery visits, agree in advance on participant numbers, the language of the excursion, transport and tasting rules. In the high-altitude areas of Bolivia and Peru, adjustment to elevation should take priority over extra evening activities: excessive alcohol can interfere with well-being and rest. Discuss any personal altitude-related medical concerns with a doctor before traveling.

The selected program has six principal countries. Entry, transit and documentation must therefore be checked for each traveler's citizenship **in all six**, including Argentina, Chile and Bolivia. Food and drinks not listed among the included services remain a personal choice. For independent restaurant visits, consider the preferences and dietary restrictions of everyone in the group.

We can discuss adding culinary days or creating a separate winery route. That requires a new plan with named cities, visit availability and timing. The existing itinerary is a useful starting point, not an already confirmed series of tastings.

## Frequently asked questions about food and wine in Brazil, Peru and Uruguay

### Are wineries in Uruguay included?

No. The Uruguay stage of the existing 20-day tour is a one-day [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) excursion by ferry from Buenos Aires and back. Visiting Tannat wineries requires separate arrangements for route, transport and time.

### Where is a wine tasting actually offered?

An optional winery excursion in the Maipo Valley, **Chile**, is available. The stated cost is **$230 per person, minimum 2 participants**. It is an optional addition to the six-country tour, not an included tasting in one of the three countries in the heading.

### Is dinner in Buenos Aires included?

Yes. The itinerary includes a tango show with dinner in Argentina. This culinary component enriches the journey but does not turn sightseeing days in Brazil, Uruguay and Peru into specialist food excursions.

### Can I try Peruvian ceviche on the standard itinerary?

In [Lima](/peru/place/lima/), you can choose a restaurant serving ceviche and other local dishes if free time permits. But the existing program has no special ceviche tasting or confirmed ceviche restaurant. Such a meal can be planned separately.

### Can the trip focus solely on these three countries and food?

The existing [20-day tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) crosses six countries. A food-focused Brazil–Uruguay–Peru route would be a different program, requiring fresh choices of flights, duration and culinary visits.

lead: >-
  Iguazú Falls in Brazil and high-altitude Lake Titicaca in Peru offer two principal nature experiences. In Uruguay, our itineraries include a one-day ferry excursion from Buenos Aires to Montevideo, so a separate nature-focused route through the country is not part of the offer.
---

## Nature tours through Brazil, Peru and Uruguay

Our selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. Both itineraries connect [Brazil](/brazil/), [Peru](/peru/) and [Uruguay](/uruguay/) with other South American countries. [“Six Latin American Countries in 20 Days: From Rio to Machu Picchu”](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) visits Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Chile, Bolivia and Peru. [“Eight South American Countries in 32 Days”](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/) also includes Ecuador and Colombia.

The nature experiences in the three selected countries are distributed unevenly. Brazil's standout destination is Iguazú Falls; Peru offers the high-altitude landscape around Lake Titicaca and the Andes. Uruguay contributes a visit to Montevideo. This is an important distinction: **selecting the nature theme on a multi-country journey does not turn every country along the route into a separate ecotour**.

## Brazil: Iguazú Falls and the hills above Rio

The Brazilian stages of both tours include Rio de Janeiro and the [Iguazú area](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/). In Rio, visitors explore Corcovado and Sugarloaf Mountain. These urban excursions provide views of the bay, coastline and forested hills, combining natural scenery with renowned cultural landmarks.

The [32-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/) visits the Brazilian and Argentine sides of Iguazú Falls on separate days. The Brazilian side offers broad panoramas of the cascades, while the Argentine side has its own network of walking routes. **The Bird Park and Macuco Safari boat excursion are optional paid activities**, so they must not be presented as part of the included price or mandatory program.

The waterfalls lie within a protected nature area with humid forest. Rainfall affects the volume of water and access to some trails. Non-slip shoes and waterproof protection for equipment are useful. Access to particular trails depends on park rules and weather conditions.

## Uruguay: Montevideo instead of a separate nature stage

Both itineraries feature **a one-day trip to Montevideo** from Buenos Aires. It includes a ferry, city sightseeing and a return to Argentina. [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) introduces visitors to the city's history, architecture and waterfront atmosphere, but neither tour visits a Uruguayan national park as a separate activity.

It would be wrong to suggest that included excursions cover Uruguayan grasslands, marine reserves or wild animals merely because Uruguay appears in the geographical filter. If the country's nature is your main objective, different stops and extra travel time would be required.

For the existing options, the ferry timetable, documents for leaving and re-entering Argentina, sightseeing duration and possible weather-related disruption are important. Ferry costs and whether they are included should be checked for the specific tour.

## Peru: Titicaca and Machu Picchu

Peru comes in the second half of both journeys. After Bolivia's highlands, travelers head to Puno and [Lake Titicaca](/peru/place/puno-and-lake-titicaca/), then through mountainous areas to [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/), Machu Picchu and Lima.

Lake Titicaca lies at approximately 3,810 meters above sea level. On the [32-day route](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/), the [Uros Islands](/peru/place/uros-islands/) are visited in the afternoon following the crossing from Bolivia into Peru. This is not an extended expedition across the entire lake; the difference between a short excursion and a prolonged stay on the water matters.

Machu Picchu stands amid steep Andean slopes. The included excursion introduces the historical site and mountain landscape, but does not itself imply multi-day trekking on high-altitude trails. When booking, check the admission-ticket type, train departure time and physical demands.

Altitude affects travelers differently. Plan according to previous overnight locations, travel pace and rest time, particularly if there are medical restrictions.

## Comparing 20 days and 32 days

| Question | 20-day itinerary | 32-day itinerary |
|---|---|---|
| Principal countries | 6 | 8 |
| Brazil | Rio and Iguazú | Rio and Iguazú |
| Uruguay | Day in Montevideo | Day in Montevideo |
| Peru | Puno, Cusco and Machu Picchu | Titicaca, Cusco, Machu Picchu and Lima |
| After Peru | End of the itinerary | Ecuador, Galápagos and Colombia |

The [20-day journey](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) suits travelers who want to combine major destinations in several countries without continuing to the Galápagos and Colombia. The [32-day version](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/) has broader nature geography but adds more flights and climate changes.

Paying for a longer trip makes sense if the extra countries genuinely align with your goals. For waterfalls, lakes and highlands, count the days spent at the actual sites, not simply the time between the first and last flights.

## What to check before choosing

Rio and Iguazú are hot and humid, whereas Puno and Cusco call for cooler highland clothing. Pack comfortable shoes for the waterfall paths, protection from intense sun at altitude and luggage suitable for domestic flights.

Check separately whether excursions on both sides of Iguazú are included, which tickets cost extra, the terms of the Montevideo excursion and the exact Lake Titicaca stops. Entry rules depend on nationality and the order of border crossings. Ada Tours helps design and coordinate the itinerary against real tickets and dates.

More itineraries featuring nature attractions can be found in the [multi-country nature travel catalog](/multi-country/interests/nature/).

## Frequently asked questions about nature journeys through Brazil, Peru and Uruguay

### Is a Uruguayan nature park included on these tours?

No. Both programs feature city sightseeing in Montevideo. Visiting Uruguay's nature areas would require a separate itinerary change.

### Is Macuco Safari at Iguazú included?

On the 32-day program, the Macuco Safari boat excursion and Bird Park are optional activities offered at an additional cost. They should not be counted as part of the included excursion package.

### Can Iguazú and Lake Titicaca be combined?

Yes, both feature on the [existing multi-country routes](/multi-country/). Other countries and transfers lie between them, so assess the full trip duration.

### Which is harder: walking at Iguazú or Peru's highlands?

These involve different demands. At Iguazú, humidity, heat and wet walkways matter; in Peru, altitude and acclimatization are the main concerns. Preparation depends on health and the actual excursions.

buttonLabel: "Explore wildlife and nature in Brazil, Peru and Uruguay"
lead: >-
  Brazil's Iguazú Falls and Tijuca Forest, high-altitude Lake Titicaca in Peru and a one-day visit to Montevideo offer very different nature experiences on a major journey. Included wildlife observation on the 32-day tour is scheduled in the Galápagos, Ecuador, outside the three selected countries. In Brazil, the Bird Park is an optional stop; in Peru, the main lake excursion visits the Uros Islands; and in Uruguay, the program is urban. Compare the 20- and 32-day routes and see which nature experiences are included and which are optional.
---

## Nature in Brazil, Peru and Uruguay: what the real itineraries include

The wildlife-watching selection features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} — the [32-day journey through eight countries](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/), with included Galápagos wildlife excursions. To compare natural landscapes, we also discuss the [20-day tour through six countries](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) below; that tour does not offer a separate dedicated wildlife-watching program. Both routes include [Brazil](/brazil/), [Peru](/peru/) and [Uruguay](/uruguay/) as principal countries, but **neither journey is limited to these three**. Between Brazil and Peru lie Argentina, Chile and Bolivia. The longer option also visits Ecuador and Colombia after Peru.

Landscapes and wildlife watching are different travel goals. On the 32-day program, dedicated animal observation takes place in Ecuador's Galápagos, whereas scenic views and city excursions dominate in the three selected countries. Confirmed excursions can be summarized as follows:

| Country | Nature attractions and format |
|---|---|
| Brazil | Tijuca Forest and Iguazú Falls; Bird Park and Macuco Safari are optional |
| Peru | Lake Titicaca, excursion to the Uros reed islands, mountain scenery |
| Uruguay | Day in Montevideo, city sightseeing without a nature reserve |

For travelers whose goal is watching birds and other animals, it is important to distinguish scenic landscapes from excursions specifically designed for wildlife observation. Water, forest or even “national park” in a stop's name does not prove that the excursion includes searching for animals.

## Brazil: from Tijuca's tropical forest to Iguazú

Brazil's nature scenery begins in [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/). On the way to Corcovado, visitors pass through the tropical vegetation of [Tijuca National Park](/brazil/), while the hills offer panoramas of the bay, forested slopes and city. This day's main excursion is to Corcovado and Christ the Redeemer; it does not replace a separate walk along the park's nature trails.

The next major nature attraction is [Iguazú Falls](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/). The Brazilian side offers wide panoramas of the cascades, with a guided walk along designated paths included in the ordinary program. The group then visits the Argentine side. The waterfalls are situated in protected parks with humid subtropical forest; standard excursions focus on the cascades and different views of the water.

The [Bird Park](/brazil/place/parque-das-aves/) is near the falls. It can be added, but it is **optional and separately charged**. The same applies to Macuco Safari, combining a journey through forest with a boat trip towards the Iguazú cascades. Despite its name, it is not a specialist safari focused on observing wild animals. Decide in advance whether these extra activities matter to you, and check their actual content and price.

## Peru: Lake Titicaca and the Andes' natural environment

Both tours include [Lake Titicaca](/peru/place/puno-and-lake-titicaca/) on the Peruvian stage. The lake's high-altitude scenery is combined with a visit to the [Uros Islands](/peru/place/uros-islands/), where travelers discover reed structures and the lake communities' traditions.

Titicaca is an aquatic ecosystem with reed beds and birdlife, but no specialized, extended birdwatching is included in the confirmed program. The main focus of the standard excursion is the islands and their inhabitants. Targeted bird photography, an extra boat trip or visits to different natural areas require separate arrangements.

The journey then continues through [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/), [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/) and Lima. The Peruvian Andes provide beautiful mountain views, but these days focus on history, archaeology and urban culture. They must not be presented as separate safaris in Peruvian national parks.

## Uruguay: Montevideo for one day

[Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) is included on both tours as a day trip by ferry from Buenos Aires. After arrival, travelers enjoy city sightseeing, including [Independence Square](/uruguay/place/montevideo-independence-square/), the [Old Town](/uruguay/place/montevideo-old-town/), [port](/uruguay/place/montevideo-port/) and other urban landmarks. The group returns to Argentina in the evening.

The day offers an opportunity to see the Río de la Plata estuary and get to know Uruguay, but **no nature safari, birdwatching, marine wildlife trip or nature-reserve visit is listed**. Travelers hoping to explore Uruguay's natural coastline would need to extend the itinerary with additional days. The current city tour does not include that.

## Which animals may be seen in other countries on both tours?

The full list of countries is important when assessing nature experiences. In Bolivia, both itineraries pass [Laguna Colorada](/bolivia/place/laguna-colorada/) and other high-altitude lakes, where flamingos may be seen. This is among the most specific opportunities to observe birds along the journey. The itinerary also includes Uyuni Salt Flat and Altiplano desert scenery.

The **32-day itinerary** has one particularly important advantage for wildlife enthusiasts: after Peru, it continues to Ecuador and the Galápagos Islands. Island nature excursions introduce a distinct ecosystem and animals that would never be encountered on a Montevideo sightseeing day or at Rio's city landmarks. The Galápagos, however, belong to Ecuador, not to the three selected countries.

The **20-day tour** ends in Lima. It also offers significant nature attractions — Iguazú, Bolivia's high-altitude lagoons and Titicaca — but has no Galápagos stage.

## Choosing 20 or 32 days for nature experiences

The choice depends on your precise goal. If you principally want to see Iguazú Falls, high-altitude Andean landscapes and Titicaca, both programs include those stages. Their duration and overall geography differ considerably, but the selected stops in Brazil, Peru and Uruguay are broadly similar.

If wildlife in different ecosystems is your primary interest, **the 32-day journey** offers more opportunities thanks to Ecuador and the Galápagos. It also requires more time and more complex logistics. In neither version should the optional Iguazú Bird Park automatically be treated as included.

## Weather, borders and preparation for wildlife watching

The climate across these longer journeys ranges from humid tropical forest to cool highlands. Waterproof gear helps at Iguazú, layered wind protection in the Andes, and comfortable shoes during city walks. Binoculars and a telephoto lens are useful for wildlife photography; protected areas require following park rules and keeping a safe distance from animals.

Both programs involve returning from Uruguay to Argentina, then continuing to Chile, Bolivia and Peru. Before purchasing tickets, check visa and transit requirements for every nationality, including re-entry. Service inclusions, transport conditions and the feasibility of optional excursions need confirmation for the actual travel dates.

For wildlife-focused travel, allowing more time for nature stops is usually more useful than increasing the number of countries. The existing itinerary works for a broad overview, while specialist wildlife activities can be discussed separately.

## Frequently asked questions about nature in Brazil, Peru and Uruguay

### Is Iguazú Bird Park included in both tours?

The [Bird Park](/brazil/place/parque-das-aves/) is listed as an extra excursion. Book it separately: including Iguazú on the itinerary does not automatically include a park visit.

### Where can flamingos be seen on these routes?

In Bolivia's highlands, including [Laguna Colorada](/bolivia/place/laguna-colorada/). Bolivia is part of both tours, though it does not appear in this three-country selection's name.

### Is birdwatching planned on Lake Titicaca?

A visit to the [Uros Islands](/peru/place/uros-islands/) is confirmed. Specialist birdwatching on the lake would require a separate plan.

### Does the program include a Uruguayan nature reserve?

No. Both programs include one-day sightseeing in [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/), returning to Argentina in the evening.

### Why is the 32-day program more interesting for wildlife lovers?

It continues after Peru into Ecuador, including the Galápagos Islands. The [20-day trip](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) does not include that stage.

## Brazil and Uruguay: which journey actually shows both countries?

**If you want to experience Uruguay as well as Brazil, check how many days the itinerary allocates to Uruguayan cities and the coast.** Some programs include [Colonia del Sacramento](/uruguay/place/colonia-del-sacramento/), [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) and several seaside days at [Punta del Este](/uruguay/place/punta-del-este/). Others offer only a short outing from Buenos Aires, while most of the journey is devoted to Argentine Patagonia, Iguazú or Brazil.

Our catalog includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with **both Brazil and Uruguay listed as main countries**. That does not mean the trips visit only those two countries. Current tours also include Argentina, Chile or Paraguay, and the precise list of countries differs from one program to another.

Brazil and Uruguay share a land border. Even so, **none of the four current itineraries in this selection is organized as a simple drive between their border towns**. Some travel through Argentina and across the Río de la Plata; another passes through Paraguay and reaches the Brazilian side of Iguazú. That sequence determines the paperwork, transport and actual journey duration.

## Four programs: where will you spend more time in Uruguay?

| Program | Uruguay's role |
|---|---|
| 13 days, three countries | Colonia, Montevideo, beaches |
| 16 days, Uruguay and Paraguay | Extended Uruguayan stage |
| 17 days, four countries | Excursion to Montevideo |
| 26 days, Argentina and Patagonia | One-day visit |

The [13-day Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay tour](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-uruguay-13-days/) starts in [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/) and Iguazú, then continues to Buenos Aires. Travelers cross the Río de la Plata from the Argentine capital to Colonia del Sacramento and Montevideo. The next stage is Punta del Este, with several overnight stays. This itinerary is particularly well suited to travelers who want more than a quick visit and would like a distinct Uruguayan part with time by the ocean.

The [16-day Uruguay and Paraguay tour](/multi-country/tour/uruguay-paraguay-16-days-2026/) works differently. It begins with Montevideo, historic Colonia, the wine-growing area of [Canelones](/uruguay/place/canelones/) and Punta del Este, then continues to [Asunción](/paraguay/place/asuncion/) and the Paraguayan Chaco. The last section takes travelers towards [Foz do Iguaçu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/). Its main Brazilian experience centers on the waterfalls rather than Rio or Brazil's beach coast. Argentina may also feature as an optional visit to the other side of the falls, but is not a main country of this tour.

The [17-day Brazil, Argentina, Chile and Uruguay route](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-uruguay/) emphasizes Patagonia, Buenos Aires, Iguazú and Rio. Uruguay gets a day in Montevideo; the journey then continues in Brazil and ends with a seaside stay in [Búzios](/brazil/place/buzios/). This is a broad South American overview, with Uruguay as one stop rather than a long independent holiday.

The [26-day Argentina and Patagonia tour](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-patagonia-26-days/) includes a Montevideo trip from Buenos Aires and the Brazilian side of Iguazú. Almost the entire journey, however, focuses on Argentine geography: the northwest, wine regions, Bariloche's lakes, glaciers, El Chaltén and Ushuaia, along with Chile's Torres del Paine. It would be a poor choice for exploring Uruguay in depth.

## Montevideo, Colonia and Punta del Este: how the stops differ

[Colonia del Sacramento](/uruguay/place/colonia-del-sacramento/) stands on the Río de la Plata. Its historic quarter is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Cobbled streets, low old buildings, bastions and a lighthouse make Colonia a convenient stop between Buenos Aires and Montevideo. A day visit can cover a compact set of streets and viewpoints; allow an overnight stay if you want an unhurried evening walk.

[Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) is the capital, with its long waterfront Rambla, historic center, Independence Square and port districts. The [Old Town](/uruguay/place/montevideo-old-town/) contains buildings from different periods, while [Independence Square](/uruguay/place/montevideo-independence-square/) is a convenient place to begin sightseeing. On a short visit, decide whether architecture and museums, waterfront walks or local food matter most.

[Punta del Este](/uruguay/place/punta-del-este/) offers a different format: the Atlantic Ocean, beaches, seaside walks, restaurants and time without mandatory excursions. Playa Mansa and Playa Brava differ in their exposure to the sea. The resort is especially lively during the Southern Hemisphere summer, when visitor numbers and accommodation demand rise. Several nights in Punta del Este therefore create an entirely different impression of Uruguay from a single visit to Montevideo.

In [Canelones](/uruguay/place/canelones/), the program may include a wine component. Uruguay is known for wines made from the Tannat grape, but a tasting is included only where it is expressly specified in the individual itinerary. Merely mentioning a wine region does not make tastings part of the tour.

## Via Argentina: ferries and border formalities

For a combination of Rio, Iguazú, Buenos Aires and Uruguay, a practical sequence commonly passes through Argentina. On the 13-day tour, Brazil comes first, then Buenos Aires and the Río de la Plata crossing. The ferry timetable and border-processing arrangements must be checked for the particular sailing. Immigration control may take place before boarding; exact location and timing depend on the operator and route.

On the 17- and 26-day options, the Montevideo visit is shorter. It is especially important to compare ferry duration, time in the city and the return journey. “One day in Uruguay” does not mean a full free day in Montevideo: transport and formalities inevitably take time.

The itinerary via Paraguay goes in the opposite direction: Uruguay first, then Asunción and other Paraguayan regions, ending at Iguazú in Brazil. Thus the order of countries in a catalog title should not be mistaken for the sequence of arrivals and departures. Planning requires exact cities, dates, means of transport and border checkpoints.

## Documents for Brazil, Uruguay and transit countries

Visa and entry conditions depend on nationality and passport type. Uruguay's Ministry of the Interior publishes the visa regime by nationality, while the country's Ministry of Foreign Affairs explains consular procedures. Brazil has separate requirements. Travel through Buenos Aires also requires checking Argentina; longer programs may involve Chile and Paraguay.

**Check not only whether a visa is required, but also how many entries are permitted.** A ferry trip from Argentina to Uruguay and back crosses the Argentine border again. The same issue arises when a traveler returns from one side of Iguazú Falls to the other. A single-entry authorization, when restricted by document type, may not cover the required sequence. Even a day trip to Montevideo involves ordinary Uruguayan entry formalities despite the lack of an overnight stay.

Before paying for the trip, prepare a simple outline: each traveler's nationality and passport, entry and exit points, how often each border is crossed, document validity and any transit through a third country. Ada Tours helps match this to the itinerary. Final requirements should be checked against current rules from the competent authorities for the actual dates.

## Money and bank cards along the route

Brazil uses the Brazilian real (BRL); Uruguay uses the Uruguayan peso (UYU). The Central Bank of Uruguay confirms the Uruguayan peso as the country's legal tender. Argentina has its own peso; a trip through Paraguay also involves the guaraní, and a visit to Chile the Chilean peso.

US dollars can be a useful reserve for exchange but should not be treated as a universal currency for local shops and services. International cards are widely used in large cities, while small purchases, markets and journeys outside major centers may require cash. Use authorized exchange providers and retain receipts where required.

Visa and Mastercard cards issued by Russian banks generally do not work abroad because of restrictions in international payment networks. Cards issued by foreign banks should be checked with the issuer for fees, supported currencies and cash-withdrawal availability. With several countries on one itinerary, a backup payment method is essential: one card or a wad of dollars cannot be guaranteed to cover every expense.

## When to travel: Uruguayan beaches and Brazilian weather

Southern Hemisphere summer runs from December through February. Punta del Este is busy during this period, while Rio can be hot and humid with episodes of heavy rain. Water levels at Iguazú Falls and trail conditions depend on rainfall, so conditions may change abruptly even during one journey.

If the itinerary includes Chile and Patagonia, you will also need clothes for cool, windy areas. Packing according only to the forecast for Rio is not enough. Layers, light waterproof outerwear, comfortable shoes for wet paths and separate beach clothing make sense.

Decide what matters most: summer swimming in Uruguay, cultural sightseeing, waterfalls or a longer journey through Patagonia. This will influence your choice of itinerary more than the formal number of countries.

## Frequently asked questions about travel through Brazil and Uruguay

### Can I visit Brazil and Uruguay without Argentina?

The two countries share a border, so such a trip is geographically possible. Current tours in this selection are arranged differently: routes including Rio and Uruguay pass through Argentina, while the larger Uruguay–Paraguay tour enters Brazil from Paraguay. An itinerary restricted to two countries needs separate transport planning.

### How many days do I need to get to know Uruguay properly?

A short Montevideo visit covers several landmarks but leaves little time for Colonia and the beaches. For a meaningful introduction, choose a program with several stops and overnight stays in Uruguay. Among the current options, the 13- and 16-day itineraries provide this.

### What is the difference between Colonia and Montevideo?

Colonia is known for its compact historic quarter and old architecture on the Río de la Plata. Montevideo is a capital with museums, squares, a long Rambla and contemporary city life. They complement each other but are not interchangeable excursions.

### Do the tours include beach holidays?

Yes. The 13-day itinerary includes several days in Punta del Este, and the 17-day program ends with a stay in Brazil's Búzios. The 26-day journey and the Paraguay option have different priorities. Check the actual daily schedule, not just the countries in the heading.

### Do I need a separate visa for Uruguay?

It depends on citizenship and passport type. Uruguay's Ministry of the Interior publishes official entry rules. If traveling via Argentina, check repeat-entry rights; via Paraguay and Chile, check each country's requirements.

### Can I pay everywhere by card?

No particular card can be guaranteed to work in every city or at every stage. Russian-issued Visa and Mastercard cards do not work abroad, while foreign-issued cards may have restrictions and fees. Plan cash and currency exchange in advance.
